findings.summary: Agent-based modeling (ABM) is a computational simulation approach that represents a system as numerous autonomous agents interacting within a shared environment. Each agent follows simple decision-making rules or heuristics, and system-level patterns emerge from their simultaneous interactions. ABMs are used across biology, ecology, and social science to explore how micro-level behaviors generate macro-level outcomes. The approach originated in the late 1940s with theoretical machines, expanded through 1970s segregation and colony models, and saw major growth in the 1990s with large-scale simulations like Sugarscape. ABMs are typically implemented as computer simulations using custom software or toolkits to test how changes in individual behavior affect overall system dynamics.

mechanisms.title: Emergent pattern formation
mechanisms.explanation: System-level properties arise from the simultaneous interactions of many simple agents following local rules, without centralized control. Higher-level patterns such as aggregation, segregation, or cultural diffusion emerge from these bottom-up interactions.

mechanisms.title: Rule-based agent decision making
mechanisms.explanation: Individual agents are characterized as boundedly rational, acting according to perceived self-interest using heuristics or simple decision rules. Agents may also exhibit learning, adaptation, and reproduction within the simulation environment.

unknowns: Precise mapping between specific agent heuristics and observed macro-scale outcomes
Details of environment-agent interaction topology beyond basic interaction networks
Algorithmic implementation specifics of learning and adaptation processes within agents
Complete characterization of how simple rules scale to produce complex system behaviors in all domains
